fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Sleeping Emperors and Mythic Ancestors", "body": "McIntosh describes the interface between history and myth as a lifelong fascination, noting how national heroes turn into mythical figures almost at once. His German example is the emperor Frederick Barbarossa, said to sleep in a cave in the Kyffhauser range in Thuringia, waking every hundred years to ask a dwarf whether the ravens still circle the mountain. When Bismarck unified Germany in 1871, a huge monument to Wilhelm the First went up there with Barbarossa and a raven at its base. He also traces the older lineage back to Tuisto, cognate with the Sanskrit sky god Dyaus, whose son Mannus fathered three German tribes and gave Mannheim its name."}, {"title": "A Country That Forgot Its Own Grail", "body": "Teaching English at the University of Bremen, McIntosh asked a class what the Holy Grail was, and only one young man ventured that it had something to do with rejuvenation and the quest for eternal life. He calls that a pity, since Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival is one of the great medieval epics and Wagner returned to the Grail in Parsifal and Lohengrin. Chance reads the passage where the Grail is not a Christian relic but a stone whose name a heathen read clearly in the constellations. McIntosh offers one speculative theory that the Grail recalls an ancient asteroid crater in what is now the Czech Republic."}, {"title": "Vulture Bone Flutes and Golden Cone Hats", "body": "Against the idea that prehistoric northern Europeans were primitive people without culture, McIntosh points to the Nebra sky disc, which he describes as essentially a lunar calendar probably used for agriculture, and to far older finds: the Venus of Willendorf, a large breasted statuette some 30,000 years old found in Austria in the early twentieth century, and a flute carved from a vulture's bone roughly 35,000 years old. He notes the archaeologist Marija Gimbutas argued such figures evidence an early matriarchal culture in Europe. Chance raises the golden conical hats; McIntosh suggests the cone may serve a purpose similar to a bishop's mitre."}, {"title": "Spirituality Brought Down Through the Hands", "body": "The thread McIntosh calls distinctly German is the marriage of the spiritual with the material. Hildegard of Bingen was an abbess, physician, herbalist, composer and painter whose remedies, he says, were imparted to her in visions, and who repeatedly got into trouble with the church yet argued her way out. Paracelsus wrote as much theology as medicine, Jacob Boehme wrote in alchemical metaphor, and the poet Novalis worked as a mining engineer. Rudolf Steiner, who placed himself in the Rosicrucian line, insisted spirituality be brought into the physical world, yielding homeopathic remedies, biodynamic agriculture, Waldorf schools and eurythmy."}, {"title": "Abraxas, Loki and the Union of Opposites", "body": "Chance argues the deepest thread in Occult Germany is the union of opposites, contending that the church's split of an authorized god of light from a devil produced a sterilizing, anti life force. He cites Hermann Hesse's novel Demian, where Abraxas is both god and devil, and Jung's Seven Sermons to the Dead, where Abraxas is effectiveness itself, a power that non power cannot cancel out. McIntosh agrees that element is suppressed in the Christian scheme and offers Loki, the Nordic trickster who is still part of the universe, the grain of sand in the oyster."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Dr. Christopher McIntosh joins InnerVerse to discuss his new book, Occult Germany, a work inspired by his love and fascination for the mystical secrets of this ancient nation. Tune in to walk the line between history and myth, as we discover Parzival and the Holy Grail and other sacred Germanic relics, consider Abraxas & the alchemical union of opposites, search for the Roman roots of Germanophobia, and find synchronicity with Saxon beliefs and the universal religion.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, you'll hear about the Irminsul, sacred trees, and the crucified savior, mystical water rites of Easter, the Odic force and Orgone energy, Rosicrucian mirror magic technology, Wagner and sacred festival dramas, the ups & downs of German Neo-Paganism, and universal vs. local truths. All that and much more!

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Irminsul and the Felled Sacred Centers", "body": "McIntosh describes the Irminsul as the sacred pillar or tree of the Saxons, destroyed on Charlemagne's order around 772, and points to a carving on the Externsteine cliffs that appears to show it bowing before the Christian cross. He compares its curling branches and chevroned trunk to Assyrian and Babylonian world trees, while Chance reads it as evidence of a crucified savior motif older than Christianity. McIntosh cautions that sul means pillar rather than sun, ties the name to the Irminones tribe, and recounts the English missionary Boniface cutting down the Donar Oak at Geismar."}, {"title": "Why Trees Live So Deep in the German Psyche", "body": "Quoting a teasing proverb about Germans, sausages and trees, McIntosh traces a reverence for trees back to Nordic cosmology, where the universe itself is the tree Yggdrasil, Odin hangs on it for nine days and nights to win the runes, and the first humans, Ask and Embla, descend from an ash and an elm. He follows the thread forward to the Christmas tree and to forester Peter Wohlleben, whose book describes trees with distinct personalities that decide whether to store rainfall for drought or spend it on growth, which changed how McIntosh walks through his local wood."}, {"title": "Water, Memory and the Silent Easter Spring", "body": "Chance links Bacchus to the German word bach, meaning stream, and argues the sun and water depend on each other, since without the sun water would be solid ice. McIntosh explains Viktor Schauberger's insight that logs travel better down curving, undulating channels, and describes Wasserschöpfen, the Easter custom of drawing spring water in complete silence so it keeps a special potency all year. Chance cites Veda Austin's partial freezing experiments and the Hebrew letter mem, and McIntosh recalls a Berlin exhibition where saliva drops turned chaotic after a mobile phone call."}, {"title": "The Odic Force, Rediscovered Again and Again", "body": "McIntosh presents the life force as an idea found and lost repeatedly: Mesmer's animal magnetism, the Odic force of the industrialist Baron Reichenbach, Wilhelm Reich's work, the Chinese chi and Indian prana, and Rupert Sheldrake's morphic resonance. Chance connects it to his own biofield tuning practice, and McIntosh speaks of benevolent energies at particular spots in the garden he is building in Lower Saxony. Chance then raises the old word for stork, and McIntosh explains the stork as bearer of the Od, carrying new souls from the fountain at the foot of the world tree."}, {"title": "Rosicrucian Mirrors, Orbs and a Rooted Paganism", "body": "McIntosh connects the mirrors found in Christian Rosenkreuz's rediscovered tomb to a shiny cylindrical device built by scientists near Novosibirsk, said to enable telepathy across great distances and echo Siberian shamanic experience. Chance recounts seeing beach ball sized orbs with two witnesses on the day of the 2017 eclipse. Turning to Wagner's sacred festival dramas and the neo-pagan revival, McIntosh argues paganism can never become a mass movement because it has no creed, praises Iceland's undogmatic community, and insists nature religion stays rooted in place, while Chance defends syncretism as the search for universal truth."}]
